name: DBMS Basics
description: Core DBMS concepts for semester and GATE revision.

cards.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the four guarantees a transaction should give.
A transaction happens completely or not at all. If any part fails, every change it made is rolled back.
Once a transaction commits, its changes survive crashes and power loss (usually via a write-ahead log on disk).
A candidate key is any minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row. The primary key is the one candidate key chosen to identify rows; it can't be NULL.
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row. A candidate key is a superkey with nothing removable.

cards.front: What does a foreign key constraint guarantee?
cards.back: Every non-NULL value in the referencing column matches an existing key in the referenced table (referential integrity).
When every attribute holds a single, atomic value — no repeating groups or lists inside one cell.
When it is in 1NF and no non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key (no partial dependencies).
When it is in 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (no transitive dependencies on the key).

cards.front: What extra condition does BCNF add over 3NF?
cards.back: For every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a superkey. 3NF allows an exception when Y is part of a candidate key; BCNF doesn't.

cards.front: What is a functional dependency X → Y?
cards.back: Whenever two rows agree on the attributes X, they must also agree on Y.
Reading data written by another transaction that hasn't committed yet — it may still be rolled back.
Running the same range query twice in one transaction and getting a different set of rows, because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.

cards.front: Which SQL isolation level prevents dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads?
cards.back: SERIALIZABLE.
A growing phase where a transaction only acquires locks, then a shrinking phase where it only releases them. This guarantees conflict-serializable schedules.

cards.front: What is the purpose of an index on a column?
cards.back: To find rows by that column's value without scanning the whole table, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.

cards.front: Why are B+ trees common for database indexes?
cards.back: They stay balanced, have a high fan-out (few disk reads per lookup) and keep leaves linked in order, which makes range scans fast.

cards.front: What does a natural join match on?
cards.back: All columns with the same name in both tables, keeping one copy of each matched column.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates like COUNT(*).
A log where changes are recorded before they are applied to the data files, so the database can redo or undo work after a crash.
